20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Catching an imposter: candidate (left) refuses to place their hand in front of their face because it would blow their AI cover. (right) The interviewer illustrates the request. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10cd3c61-d196-4823-8c1c-fb223a3afddd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>More in our deepdive</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such incidents are becoming more common at US, UK and EU companies which hire for remote roles:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“There are a lot more fake candidates applying, leveraging AI for not just resumes, but also interviews. In extreme cases, the interviews are being outsourced so that a different person shows up for the interview. It feels a bit like playing captcha with them during interviews.”</span><em><span> – Senior EM, private-equity backed company, Bay Area, US</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“The second person we interviewed was clearly a North Korean scammer, writing questions into an LLM, reading the response, easily tripped up, and other interviews were background noise in the room.”</span><em><span> – Staff Engineer, UK</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Many applicants that looked a good fit turned out to be someone else in the Asia Pacific region doing interviews with an AI in the background. It’s easy to spot because of the ‘lag’ in a naturally flowing conversation.”</span><em><span> – head of engineering, mid-sized company, Germany</span></em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cheating in remote interviews by using AI is also commonplace. A software engineer based in Finland told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A couple of times we saw an applicant who was using AI to answer the questions, and this was sooo weird. I honestly didn’t know how to react, so we decided to cut the interview short. We then shared a note with the recruiters on how to spot this.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Hot market for some, but tough for most</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The market appears sharply bifurcated: amazing for AI and a few specialist roles, and a major struggle for everyone else.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Some accounts from folks benefitting in the current conditions:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“The market is really good as an (AI) engineer with the right experience. </span></strong><span>I’m not actively looking but get 2–3 messages a day. When I was hiring for AI engineers at my last AI startup, the market for these folks was terrible. It’s very hard to find good talent, and people that were great on paper did poorly in interviews.”</span><em><span> – AI Engineer, 5 YOE, New York, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It seems like demand for senior positions is still there, but only if your profile really matches what the company needs. For example, I’ve been working on different data pipelines for a while, and finding such a position is relatively simple. However, breaking into anything else is not! Every startup wants to hire only people experienced in that particular thing they need.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 13 YOE, Big Tech, UK</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s what two job seekers who are struggling at present say:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“I sent my handcrafted resume to 30–40 positions, and heard back from zero.</span></strong><span> Eventually, I got an interview after a recruiter reached out via LinkedIn; I don’t know how I would’ve found anything, if it was not for this!”</span><em><span> – Software engineer, 5 YOE, Amsterdam, Netherlands</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As a developer without a specific “specialization,” I’m struggling to get any interviews. I’ve spent a few years as frontend, then another few as backend, and most recently working on DevEx. In this market, I just don’t get any callbacks for interviews, not even a first round interview.”</span><em><span> – Software engineer, 6 YOE, London, UK</span></em></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI/ML/FDE market on fire</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We see in the data that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa05bbe1-28db-460e-9d87-19deb298da44?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>AI engineering is seeing explosive demand</span></a><span>, and that forward deployed engineers (FDEs) are also seeing </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a31ab315-602f-4087-8fa5-2fd8c686a440?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>a massive spike in demand</span></a><span>. </span><em><span>For more detail on this, check our deepdive on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f7d6755c-a053-41db-8fe8-b647bdc70545?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>what FDEs are, and why they’re hot right now.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anecdotal evidence from job seekers suggests that being in these fields means the market is as good as it gets, right now:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“It’s the greatest job market I’ve ever seen. </span></strong><span>I’m an L5 former FDE, now SWE, who has worked on LLM apps for ~2 years. The inbound top of the funnel is bonkers, and I find myself saying “no” to places that I would have once killed to work at.”</span><em><span> – AI Engineer at an AI decacorn, San Francisco, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I have seen huge interest in FDEs and AI Engineers as an engineer who’s been interviewing.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 5 YOE, New York, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s not hard to get interviews as an ML/AI engineer. The technical bar is about the same as late 2022. If anything, onsites seem to be of fewer rounds for the same level. Companies seem to move fast to get candidates onsite.”</span><em><span> – ML engineer, ex-Meta, Bay Area, US</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An engineer at Apple is surprised by the demand for their skills from AI companies:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Got a lot of responses from cold applications for AI roles, and ended up with two offers at AI infra companies. I ended up getting a significant pay bump beyond what Apple offers for the same level!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A software engineer at well-known company in the Bay Area, also finds the job market is good:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I got offers for Senior SWE with Stripe and Rippling, was rejected from Snowflake… Anecdotally, the job market is better compared to 2025 for regular SWE positions in the Valley.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>EM and Staff+ profiles are near-impossible to fill</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A repeat complaint from hiring managers in the US is how challenging it is to recruit solid engineering managers and Staff+ engineers:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“It’s extremely difficult to hire EMs and Staff+ engineers.</span></strong><span> It’s much easier to hire folks with less than 10 years of experience. This is despite us offering 90th percentile comp via Pave, and having a hybrid and good culture.”</span><em><span> – Fractional VP of Engineering, Series B, New York, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“My team has been looking for a new engineering manager for three months and we barely had any good applicants. It’s a super weird dynamic right now.” </span><em><span>– Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Series D Fintech, company with offices in the US and EU</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“The most desirable candidates right now are EM or staff-level folks who can keep up with uncertainty in the business.</span></strong><span> We are having trouble hiring folks who roll with the constant change that is now very typical at startups.”</span><em><span> – CTO at a San Francisco-based startup</span></em></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>“Specialist” profiles are hard to recruit</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few examples:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Distributed systems engineers: “</span></strong><span>We can’t find enough qualified distributed systems engineers, cloud infra etc. I have 20 reqs [open positions] right now.”</span><em><span> – Recruiter at a hyperscaler, US</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Product engineers: </span></strong><span>“‘Product engineer’ has been a hard profile to find. It is also hard to find someone with a decent design eye who can also build full stack. The hardest thing to hire for has been taste + trust… I’d rather hire someone who is ‘behind’ on AI, but has great taste/judgment than someone with complex agent setups and prompt libraries.”</span><em><span> – Tech Lead, seed-stage startup, Los Angeles, US</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Senior engineers, in general: </span></strong><span>“As a hiring manager trying to hire seniors right now, it has felt pretty difficult. Most applicants are totally unqualified, and the qualified ones do poorly in an interview.”</span><em><span> – Engineering manager, robotics company, Canada</span></em></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Silence for many</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One in five respondents detail how difficult it has been to get responses from recruiters:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Things are looking bleak. Now, applications are going into a void. Recruiters aren’t reaching out immediately as before. Of 10 or so applications sent out, I’ve gotten one interview scheduled that was then rescinded because it looks like the team was laid off.”</span><em><span> – Frontend engineer, 10+ YOE, Southeast US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The job market has been a desert. I’ve gotten back into applying, job agencies seem to have few roles they’re looking to fill. The companies I have applied to myself, never reply.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 8 YOE, Southern California</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Recruiters are ghosting me! Every time when I respond to recruiter reachouts, they ALL ghosted me after a few messages and have similar stories from friends.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 7 YOE, ex-Meta, Switzerland</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“So far, I have a hard time even getting past the hiring manager and I’m rejected before I can do the proper technical assessment.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 7 YOE, Helsinki, Finland</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even folks at Big Tech face a lack of response. Here’s a Technical Program Manager currently at Meta who used to be very in-demand:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I put a few feelers out when Meta announced layoffs, and it’s just radio silence. I don’t want to sound cocky, but with my resume, you at least get a chat with a recruiter, usually right away. But Google and Anthropic just ghosted me.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Higher hiring bar & lower compensation – but not for everyone</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a “normal” market, when the hiring bar goes up, so does compensation. But we heard anecdotes about the hiring bar going up, with the compensation on offer trending down!</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Very picky hiring managers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few examples:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>Out of my last 100 or so candidates that got to the on-site interviews, we extended two offers. </span></strong><span>It’s just hard to get quality applicants for senior-level positions.”</span><em><span> – Engineering Manager, mid-sized company, hiring remote across the US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I just talked to one of my colleagues who interviewed 150+ folks for a mid-level position, and is about to give up because none clear the bar.”</span><em><span> – Director of Engineering, Big Tech, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“From 2,000 applications for software engineers and data engineers, 10-20 make it to culture fit interviews</span></strong><span>, about 3-6 make it to culture fit, and 1-2 get an offer. Our interview round has resume screening, recruiter call, and a take-home exercise, before the culture fit interview.”</span><em><span> – Recruiter, deep tech company, Helsinki, Finland</span></em></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Some AI-native companies struggling to hire in the Bay Area</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-native startups have raised large funding rounds, pay at the very top of the market – and yet some founders find it hard to recruit. Here’s a CTO at such a startup in San Francisco:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There are three groups of people we see on the market:</span></p><ol style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>People who don’t “get” AI.</span></strong><span> Enough said.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Slop cannons:”</span></strong><span> they use AI, but don’t grok fundamentals, don’t pay any attention to code quality, and think it’s okay to yolo stuff to prod because they’ve never worked on real systems</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Truly exceptional people: </span></strong><span><span>they “get” AI and have autonomy. They are either joining the AI labs, or getting Y Combinator funding and starting their own company.</span><br><br><span>It’s hard to hire!”</span></span></p></li></ol></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem seems to be that anyone who is </span><em><span>good enough</span></em><span> for this startup to recruit, also has the option to start their own company, and in San Francisco, they often do. </span><em><span>This could explain why more SF-based startups also hire remotely, even in their early stages.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Higher interview bar</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A fullstack engineer with three years of experience in the US explains:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s easy to get interviews, but the bar to pass them is higher than in 2022. For leetcode [data structure and algorithms interview], you not only have to get the optimal solution, but have to be quick too, and not fumble. Since many people can solve them because of resources like Neetcode, the bottleneck is speed.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Interviews are changing, and AI-related exercises are becoming normal. </span></strong><span>A lead fullstack engineer in Germany told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Interviews have changed, a LOT! In the past, questions would include things like React vs Angular, Java vs Go. Today it’s ‘can you one-shot a waterfall spec to derive a product in two hours that would otherwise take 10 years?’ Either you go with it and get a job offer, or you push back and explain the problems with it, and then you don’t.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A hiring manager based in Prague, Czechia, says candidates don’t do well when tested on AI skills:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We recently introduced a hiring baseline requiring AI skills, and we find a lot of the candidates have no concrete experience using AI tools.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Compensation seems lower</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few data points:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A software engineer in Southern California: “A Walmart contractor role for a remote ‘Web Engineer’ offered $140K and zero benefits (no PTO [paid time off], bonuses; no insurance).”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A principal engineer in the Southwest US: “As a principal engineer, I received a few offers for Senior-level positions that were less than I made as a Senior, pre-2020!”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A software engineer in the UK: “Pay bands are all over the place. I’ve seen some at £80k (terrible!) and others ranging from £125k–£200k (great!).”</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>One reality at present is that it’s an employer’s market, meaning they get to choose what to pay. </span></strong><span>As a founder at a seed-stage startup in the Bay Area tells us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s an employer’s market. I’m getting interest from principal engineers from Snowflake for a $250K base salary position because they got laid off.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Mid-year hiring seems to be down</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A software engineer in the US reckons there’s something about the middle of the year being quiet:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I interviewed around a little in January 2026. I always got responses from recruiters, usually within a day. Now, in June 2026, it’s night and day: my own company just cut 50% of staff at our board’s demand.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Data on the job market confirms that hiring is seasonal, and mostly happens during the first six months of the year:</span></p><div 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Recruitment shifts: Most hiring happens January-June, not July-December. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/655fa96e-2b26-4f4b-bfd0-e8510d87055c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Part 1</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sadly, offers were rescinded for a few correspondents:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I finished the process with PayPal and we were in the hiring committee phase, but they cut 20% of their workforce because of AI.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 8 YOE, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A dev I know left for a new role and got a call the week beforehand, letting them know their position was cancelled as part of layoffs. Another friend joined a mutual’s YC company and got laid off within three months.”</span><em><span> – founder, Bay Area, US</span></em></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Engineering leader & IC recruitment are equally weird</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hiring managers complain how hard it is to recruit hands-on engineering leaders, at the same time as hands-on engineering leaders find it harder than ever to get hired! It’s the same paradox as mentioned above, suggesting that on some level it’s harder for people and employers to connect these days.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A CTO in San Francisco is encountering a very weird market:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I left my CTO job at the beginning of the year. I joined another early-stage startup as a CTO, but got burnt… Anecdotally, it feels like the market is fairly ‘hot’ in head-of-eng and CTO jobs, BUT here’s the weird thing: </span><strong><span>there are now lots of engineering leaders who are either part-time contracting, or building in stealth, like me.</span></strong><span> This is because taking one of these jobs would mean taking a pay cut, or finding yourself in a higher stress/more invasive work-life balance position, post-job change.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That engineering leadership roles are being interpreted very differently doesn’t help things, either. From a head of engineering in the UK:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“I’ve seen a huge difference in specs/responsibilities for eng manager and head of eng roles. </span></strong><span>Some very hands-on with people management, and others essentially slimmed down to be an IC who happens to manage. Pay bands are all over the place… The market isn’t as good as I remember a few years ago, but it does seem buoyant, particularly for people willing to cross over a bit more and not just do pure people management or pure IC work.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. US market trends</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are some current trends in the US:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Folks experiencing the “best market ever” are in the US. </span></strong><span>These are AI engineering, ML engineers, forward-deployed engineers, and a few Big Tech folks with very strong networks. The same roles are not enjoying truly standout conditions in places like the UK and the EU – or perhaps there are just fewer of them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Product engineering demand is much stronger in the US. </span></strong><span>An AI Engineer in Europe observed that most applied AI roles are in the US, while in places like the UK, most companies hire forward-deployed engineers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>The “talent shortage” complaint is more common in the US. </span></strong><span>Startups struggling to hire senior+ engineers, and Big Tech looking for infrastructure engineers, are US-headquartered. In contrast, hiring managers at EU companies describe being overwhelmed with inbound applications, and needing to put in a lot of work to find quality applicants.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Tech layoffs seem to be flooding tech hubs in the US. </span></strong><span>Reports of hiring managers getting applications from standout engineers who were let go from places like Amazon, Microsoft, Snowflake, and similar companies are all in the US. That might be because it’s harder to execute mass layoffs in Europe, meaning that fewer occurred. Big Tech has a smaller presence in Europe, which could be a factor.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Trends in the UK, EU, & rest of the world</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are factors specific to the UK, EU, and Canada:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Ghosting” is far more common than in the US. </span></strong><span>Not hearing back from recruiters, or recruiters not responding after replying to a reachout, comes up a lot among folks in the EU. In contrast, in the US, solid software engineers seem to be getting interviews easier, it’s just harder to get an offer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Fake applicants” seem a bigger problem in Europe. </span></strong><span>The issue of “fakers” with potential links to hostile governments is mentioned mostly by EU and UK companies. It might be that such folks get caught more often in Europe, where an interviewer might be more likely to use the local language and expose a fake candidate’s own lack of language ability.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Remote roles are rare, almost everything is hybrid. </span></strong><span>The disappearance of full-remote roles is a repeated complaint in the EU.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Language is a blocker. </span></strong><span>Job seekers in Germany and Czechia report being rejected from software engineering jobs for not speaking the local language at a native level. In Czechia, a hiring manager told us of their frustration caused by having a hard requirement of only proceeding with applicants with native or high-level proficiency in the local language.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Not being able to move jobs due to a “compensation ceiling” is a problem repeatedly mentioned in the EU and Brazil. </span></strong><span>Two cases:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’m struggling to find a job that pays more than what I currently make – it’s weird. I am at the Staff level at a consultancy. So far, in eight months, I got rejected instantly, save for one screening call.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I have a friend in a similar position, also “stuck” because they cannot get a higher offer than what they make now. He is working in Amazon and so far he has gotten five interviews, likely because he has Amazon in his resume. But all offers come in well below what he makes.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, Krakow, Poland</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Compensation is the problem, and the reason I don’t bother responding to inbound opportunities. I wasn’t receiving any messages in my LinkedIn inbox until two or three weeks ago. However, all the ones with compensation listed are paying less than what I’m earning, and the ones without comp listed are lower tier companies that will probably pay low as well. Have been dismissing all the recruiters so far.”</span><em><span> – Senior fullstack engineer, 8 YOE, Brazil</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In all fairness, the reason some people are hitting this compensation ceiling is because there </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c759554-556d-4a26-83e2-65277581e99b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>are fewer “top-tier” (Tier 3) positions</span></a><span> in Europe than in the US. </span><em><span>We cover more on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c759554-556d-4a26-83e2-65277581e99b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Trimodal nature of software engineering compensation.</span></a></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was very useful to talk with people about what the hiring market is like as a job seeker or a hiring manager. Of course, data is very useful but data on the market we covered in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/655fa96e-2b26-4f4b-bfd0-e8510d87055c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Part 1</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a14312a4-0299-45c7-bc0a-0d416c4c3313?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Part 2</span></a><span> of this series doesn’t quite capture how strange today’s market is:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A small group is seeing the best-ever recruitment market: </span></strong><span>AI Engineers, ML Engineers, FDEs and a few folks with exceptional experience and connections. These engineers are more in demand than ever, getting higher compensation than ever at AI companies. For example, here’s the </span><em><span>median</span></em><span> total compensation offered by various larger tech companies:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8cd4da44-2199-4bd7-ae48-ebe6e9ffd222?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>levels.fyi</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are now paying far more than the likes of Big Tech (Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Google and other similar ones). Engineers that AI labs and other “hot” companies want to hire: these are the folks that pretty much all other AI companies are also looking for.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Most companies are finding it hard to hire senior folks, but their expectations have gone up! </span></strong><span>Finding senior engineers and engineering leaders is equally hard. What is unsaid by hiring managers is that their expectations have gone up, but how much they are willing to pay has often not! Also, the massive increase in AI-enhanced resumes does not help, and is making inbound referrals useless.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Solid software engineers are not getting responses or offers, unless via referrals. </span></strong><span>The majority of people I spoke with, who are on the job market, see it as very bad, and get few to no responses for applications they put out there; even when they do, offers can be withdrawn at the last minute.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This happens while the data shows that the number of open software engineering jobs keeps </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/655fa96e-2b26-4f4b-bfd0-e8510d87055c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>going up.</span></a><span> So, why are they not seeing more opportunities?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>My sense is that the job market is somewhat worse in the UK and EU. </span></strong><span>Job seekers complain more about ghosting and being lowballed in compensation. I wonder if some of this has to do with how all leading AI labs are headquartered in the US, and more US startups have successfully pivoted to become “AI-native.” Plus, the majority of AI funding comes from US VCs, and often to companies headquartered in the Bay Area.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As AI is the single biggest growth area in the tech industry, anyone and everyone close to this space will see more and better opportunities; be that in funding, jobs, or career advancement.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How are things for you as a hiring manager or job seeker? Please leave a comment about what you see on the market.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Foundations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All three models share the same fundamental architecture, which is a transformer-based generative neural network.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The transformer was introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need,” and at its core is a mechanism called self-attention that allows each token in a sequence (a token being a small piece of text, roughly three-quarters of a word) to weigh its relationship to every other token. This setup is shared across the three models, while the components built around it, along with the training process that shapes it, vary substantially.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Training itself involves two phases:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Pre-training is where the model learns from massive amounts of text and other data by predicting the next token, repeated billions of times over.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Post-training is where the base model gets shaped into a helpful assistant through methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Constitutional AI. We will get to them in more detail in a later section.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Each architectural fork follows a consistent pattern, where different companies faced the same design question, each made a particular architectural choice, and each choice produced user-visible behavior we can observe today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first such question concerns how to scale the model’s total capacity without proportionally increasing the cost of processing every query.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Density</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every parameter added to a model carries computational cost. In a standard dense neural network, every parameter activates for every token processed, meaning that doubling the parameter count roughly doubles the compute cost per query.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Frontier developers needed a way to escape this constraint, and the architectural question became how to scale total capacity without paying full price on every single token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Google adopted a technique called Mixture of Experts, or MoE. The Gemini 1.5 technical report identifies the model as “a sparse mixture-of-expert (MoE) Transformer-based model” that “builds on a much longer history of MoE research at Google,” with the Gemini 3 Pro model extending the same approach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In an MoE layer, instead of one massive computational block where every parameter activates for each token, the network contains many smaller experts, and a small router determines which two or three experts each token should be sent to. The total parameter count can be enormous while only a fraction is activated per token, though achieving consistent results requires careful attention to load balancing and expert specialization during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI has not explicitly confirmed whether GPT-4 uses MoE, and the GPT-4 technical report deliberately omits architecture details. The GPT-5 system details describe a different efficiency approach that we will examine in the Reasoning section, where a router selects between distinct sub-models at runtime.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Nevertheless, these architectural choices produce meaningful consequences in user experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>MoE models can pack more knowledge per dollar of compute, which contributes to Gemini’s capable handling of a wide breadth of domains. The tradeoff is increased variance, since different prompts route to different experts, and imperfect load balancing during training can leave some experts underused and weaken the model’s capacity on those topics. Dense models tend to deliver more predictable per-token behavior at the cost of being harder to scale to extreme parameter counts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The term multimodal carries different meanings depending on the architectural approach, and a precise distinction helps before we take a look at the design choices.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Two fundamentally different approaches exist for handling non-text inputs like images, audio, and video:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Sequential approach:</span></strong><span> Train a strong language model first, then add a separate encoder later that translates non-text inputs into embeddings the language model can attend to.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Native adopted the native approach from the start. The Gemini 1.0 release was designed as natively multimodal, and the 1.5 technical report demonstrates the model handling, in a single input, “10.5 hours of video at 1 frame-per-second”, and the current Gemini 3 Pro model continues this design, where the model offers “native multimodal support for text, vision, and audio inputs.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI took a different path initially, with the original GPT-4 supporting vision through a separate pipeline. GPT-4o, released in May 2024, transitioned to a unified architecture, and OpenAI’s own announcement for GPT-5.5 acknowledged that “previous multimodal models from OpenAI were essentially separate models stitched together.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Lastly, Anthropic has maintained a text-first approach with strong vision capabilities, and Claude Opus 4.8 continues to support high-resolution image input introduced in Opus 4.7 at 3.75 megapixels, particularly useful for documents, screenshots, and dense charts. Anthropic has chosen to focus on text and vision as primary input modalities while setting native audio and video aside for now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For users, this architectural difference appears most clearly when working with video. Gemini handles long video files directly, and ChatGPT does the same on its more recent models. Claude performs best with documents, screenshots, and high-fidelity images.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Context</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A context window represents the amount of input a model can attend to in a single pass, measured in tokens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Larger windows allow the model to reason over more raw material at once, though long context introduces two important challenges:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Computational cost:</span></strong><span> Attention scales roughly quadratically with sequence length, so longer windows consume significantly more compute per query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Quality degradation:</span></strong><span> Models often lose track of information mentioned earlier as the window fills, with the relevance of early context dropping over the course of a long conversation.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Google pushed hardest on raw window size. The Gemini 1.5 technical report demonstrated context up to 10 million tokens, and Gemini 3 Pro and 3.1 Pro continue to offer 1 million token context in production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Anthropic offers 1 million tokens on Claude Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5, and the company’s own documentation uses the term “context rot” to describe quality degradation in long sessions, addressed through automatic compaction that summarizes earlier portions of the conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI has taken a more conservative position on window size, with GPT-4 Turbo at 128K, focusing efficiency gains on the routing architecture covered in the Reasoning section.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: justify"><span>The practical experience differs across the three models. Loading an entire codebase or a multi-hour transcript into a single session works well with Gemini and Claude, given the larger windows available. ChatGPT is structured more around efficient routing between sub-models than around accepting massive single-prompt inputs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Long context expands the range of questions you can ask, while retrieval-augmented generation, which fetches relevant external data at query time, remains relevant when freshness and cost matter.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Alignment</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Pre-training produces a base model that has processed enormous amounts of text and learned to predict the next token. At this stage, the base model behaves as a sophisticated pattern-completer with limited regard for honesty, safety, or helpfulness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Post-training is the phase where this base model is shaped into the assistant that users interact with, and the three companies have taken substantially different approaches to this work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI built on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) throughout the development of GPT-3 and GPT-4. The approach involves three main steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Human raters compare pairs of model outputs and select the better one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Those comparisons train a reward model that captures human preferences.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The reward model is then used to fine-tune the language model toward outputs that humans prefer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The GPT-4 product page describes an additional safety reward signal incorporated into RLHF to reduce harmful outputs. For the reasoning models, OpenAI added an approach called deliberative alignment, where the model reasons about safety policies at inference time. The publicly available Model Spec describes intended behavior in detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Anthropic developed an alternative method called Constitutional AI, or CAI. Instead of relying on human raters at every step, CAI uses an explicit written constitution and has the model critique and revise its own outputs against those principles, then applies AI-generated feedback to further refine the model. In January 2026, Anthropic published a 23,000-word constitution that shapes Claude’s training across synthetic data generation, response ranking, and behavioral refinement.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Google uses RLHF with learned reward models in its post-training pipeline for Gemini, with somewhat less explicit public framing than the other two companies. The Gemini technical reports describe a multi-phase training process moving from unimodal pre-training through multimodal alignment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This architectural area also reflects a broader pattern of differing transparency choices across the three companies. The 2023 GPT-4 technical report deliberately omitted architecture details, while the 2025 GPT-5 system card describes a router, named sub-models, and safety mitigations in remarkable detail. Anthropic publishes its constitution publicly, providing a detailed view into the principles that shape Claude’s behavior. The three companies have made distinct choices about transparency, and those choices have evolved over time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For users, these training differences appear as personality. Claude tends to push back more often on edge cases because the constitution explicitly trains for that behavior. ChatGPT is often quicker to attempt a task without questioning. Gemini’s responses vary more by domain.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div justify"><span>With values addressed, the most recent architectural dimension concerns how the model thinks, an area where the three companies have converged from different directions.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Reasoning</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most recent and most consequential architectural development for the current generation of models concerns whether the model produces an answer directly or reasons explicitly through tokens before answering.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A standard chat model takes a prompt and immediately begins generating the response. A reasoning model first generates internal thinking tokens, working through the problem, and only afterward produces the final answer. The same prompt, the same underlying weights, and the same context window can produce very different inference-time compute profiles depending on which approach is used.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI built dedicated reasoning models, beginning with o1 in late 2024, followed by o3 in August 2025, and continued in GPT-5.5, which was released on April 23, 2026. The architecture includes three main components.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>GPT-5-Main</span></strong><span>, a fast, high-throughput model and the successor to GPT-4o.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>GPT-5-Thinking</span></strong><span>, a deeper reasoning model and the successor to o3.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A Real-Time Router</span></strong><span> that selects between them based on conversation type, complexity, tool needs, and explicit intent in the prompt.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI plans to integrate these capabilities into a single model in the future, though the current architecture functions as a system of models rather than as a unified single model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Anthropic pursued a different approach. Claude Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 use adaptive thinking inside a single model, where the same Claude determines for itself how long to think on each request, with summarized reasoning surfaced to developers for inspection.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Google integrated thinking into Gemini 3 through Deep Think mode and the three-level thinking system in Gemini 3.1 Pro, enabling the model to reason over text, images, audio, and video in a single thinking pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For users, this architectural difference shows up more visibly than might be expected. ChatGPT can feel inconsistent across sessions because the router may have directed two similar prompts to two different sub-models. Claude tends to feel consistent because the same model varies its reasoning depth based on the request. Gemini’s behavior shifts more with domain and modality.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: Three companies that began with very different choices at every prior dimension, including MoE versus dense architecture, native versus bolted-on multimodality, and RLHF versus Constitutional AI, have all arrived at the same approximate conclusion. Explicit reasoning tokens at inference time materially improve model performance on hard problems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we looked at five architectural dimensions, each representing a question all three frontier developers had to answer when building their models.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Density:</span></strong><span> Google adopted Mixture of Experts openly, OpenAI built routed efficiency through a different mechanism, and Anthropic kept its architectural choice private.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Multimodality:</span></strong><span> Google adopted native fusion from inception, OpenAI evolved from bolted-on vision toward a unified architecture, and Anthropic maintained a text-first approach with strong vision capabilities.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Context:</span></strong><span> Google pushed the largest windows, Anthropic invested in long sessions with explicit handling of degradation, and OpenAI emphasized routing efficiency over raw window size.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Alignment:</span></strong><span> OpenAI’s RLHF combined with the Model Spec, Anthropic’s Constitutional AI combined with its published constitution, and Google’s RLHF approach represent three distinct shaping pipelines.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Reasoning:</span></strong><span> All three companies converged on explicit reasoning tokens, despite starting from different architectural choices at every prior dimension.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When we observe one of these models behaving in a particular way, we now have a framework for asking which architectural dimension produced that behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: Kirill Bobrov

Key Activities For Sustainable Engineering Team

Dunya Kirkali

“Sometimes you need to fly high: looking at strategy, direction, and the broader system around the team. Sometimes you need to fly low: joining the details, removing friction, and helping the team through turbulence. The hard part is knowing when to change altitude.”

#Leadership Management TeamHealth

item.title: Why I Stopped Arguing With People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why I Stopped Arguing With People

Cong Wang

“Over the years I’ve slowly stopped arguing. Not because I stopped caring about being right, but because I finally understood what an argument actually is, and what it can and cannot do. Here is what changed my mind.”

#Communication Influence

item.title: Some New Agentic Patterns
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Some New Agentic Patterns

Jesse Vincent

“I want to tell you a bit about how we've started shipping some changes to internal production with an "agentic user in the loop." Letting an agent work directly with the implementer building its runloop and tooling is getting us higher-quality tools and experiences for the agent without a human in the middle of a game of telephone.”

#DevEx Agents AI
item.description: Some New Agentic Patterns

item.title: Understanding Is The New Bottleneck
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Understanding Is The New Bottleneck

Geoffrey Litt

“Hot take: I think it's still important to understand the code that our agents write! In this talk I'll explain why that's the case, and show some ideas for how to efficiently understand code. Alright, let's dive in.”

#CodeQuality AI

item.title: My Favorite Keyboards
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
My Favorite Keyboards

Fabien Sanglard

“When I started using computers, we had a Sinclair ZX Spectrum at home and a nano-reseau of Thomson MO5s at elementary school. I distinctly remember how unpleasant it was to type with them. These must have been the worst keyboards I ever used. Ever since, I have paid close attention to the keyboards I use. Here is the list of my all-time favorites.”

#Tools+Setup
