justify"><span>The result is striking. Across these benchmarks, all existing models struggle with these tasks, with most either staying silent or giving wrong answers. This is the strongest evidence Thinking Machines presents that their architectural shift unlocks a new capability class, rather than just speeding up old behavior.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Limitations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Despite the encouraging results, the research also points out the things that are still hard.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Long sessions remain a real challenge for this architecture. Continuous audio and video accumulate context very quickly. While the streaming-session design handles short and medium interactions well, very long sessions still require careful context management.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Connectivity remains a hard requirement, since streaming audio and video at low latency demands a reliable internet connection. A poor connection causes the experience to degrade significantly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Scaling the model size is constrained by latency targets, with TML-Interaction-Small being the size it is, partly because Thinking Machines’ larger pretrained models are currently too slow to serve in this setting.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Looking back, the main argument is simple. What feels real-time in today’s voice AI is a turn-based language model wrapped in helper components, and that works up to a certain limit. Thinking Machines’ bet is that the way past the limit is to make interactivity part of the model itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Two architectural choices carry most of the heavy work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Time-aligned micro-turns slice time into 200-millisecond chunks, letting the model handle input and output as continuous streams.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The two-model split pairs a fast interaction model with a slower background model that handles deep reasoning, with both sharing context.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The evidence that this is a new capability class rather than just lower latency comes from the benchmarks Thinking Machines built themselves. Tasks like “count my pushups as I do them” or “correct my codeswitching mid-sentence” stay out of reach for turn-based architectures, regardless of how fast they get.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An important takeaway is that adding a capability through external scaffolding creates a ceiling on how good that capability can get, with the scaffolding becoming the bottleneck rather than the underlying system. This pattern shows up across computing, and this research preview is one of the clearest recent illustrations of it in AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines plans to open a limited research preview in the coming months, with a wider release later this year and a research grant for interaction model research.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul item.title: The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life

Yew Jin Lim

“The best investment framework isn’t the one that maximizes returns. The best career strategy isn’t the one that eliminates risk. The best contemplative practice isn’t the one that promises instant transformation. The best framework is the one you’ll stick with. For me, that’s been a boring foundation with a laboratory on top.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life

item.title: Three Bad Managers
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Three Bad Managers

Michael Lopp

“I worked for each of these humans. They either hired or promoted me. I worked for them for many years. As is my way, I’ve vastly altered the details of each human, but the core issue I describe is the core issue. Also, each of these humans is very smart. No dummies.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Three Bad Managers

item.title: Cross-Team Pragmatics
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Cross-Team Pragmatics

Phil Calçado

“I’ve been in this industry for twenty-five years and have seen all sorts of companies and projects. You know what I have never heard? Someone saying, “You know what I really like about working here? Cross-team collaboration.””

#Leadership Communication
item.description: Cross-Team Pragmatics

item.title: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Michael Lynch

“I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

#KnowledgeManagement Guide
item.description: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Sumner Evans

“Even though it is used by a large number of popular open source projects, Conventional Commits is an actively bad standard which encourages focus on the wrong things and fails to deliver on its promises.”

#Tools+Setup

rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Even the most sophisticated AI agent in your stack starts every single message from a blank slate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The model itself sees only the text placed in front of it at that exact moment, and the rest of the conversation lives outside its awareness entirely. Whatever continuity we feel when chatting with Claude or ChatGPT is something the surrounding platform is engineering on the model’s behalf, by inserting the right context back into every call. Once we understand this crucial distinction, the entire field of agent memory becomes a very different engineering problem from what it first appears to be.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will try to understand how that architecture gets built, from the constraint that forces it to exist all the way to the tradeoffs that follow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Statelessness</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A call to a large language model follows a simple pattern. The system sends a prompt, the model returns a response, and the exchange concludes there. Each subsequent call, even one made a millisecond later, begins from a completely fresh slate. This is the API contract for every commercial LLM and reflects how transformers serve traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>When we say things like “Claude remembers our conversation from yesterday,” we are describing a property of the product rather than a property of the actual model itself. The platform writes things down on the model’s behalf, then reads them back into the prompt at exactly the right moment, so the model can reason as if it had been there all along. The intelligence resides within the model itself, while the memory resides in the system surrounding it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the model itself works this way, the next question is whether we can solve the memory problem by writing everything into the model’s view on every call? The way this approach breaks gives us a better insight into how to solve this problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Context</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every API call has a context window. It is basically the bounded slab of text that the model reads when generating its response. This includes the system prompt, the user’s current message, and anything else the developer has placed there. The model has full visibility into the contents of the window, while whatever sits outside it might as well live on a different machine.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>An obvious approach to memory involves writing the entire conversation history into the context window on every call. This works well for the first few turns of a chat. Once the conversation grows longer, however, three significant problems emerge at once:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first problem is cost. Every token in the context window is paid for on each call, in both money and latency, so a linearly growing conversation produces a linearly growing bill. By message eighty, the system might be re-sending tens of thousands of tokens on every turn just to maintain continuity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second problem is latency. Larger contexts take longer to process, and a model that responds in two seconds on a short prompt may take ten or fifteen on one that has filled most of its window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third problem is the most counterintuitive of the three. The model’s attention degrades inside long contexts, and information placed in the middle of a long prompt is recalled less reliably than information at the beginning or the end. Researchers refer to this as the lost-in-the-middle effect.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Hierarchy</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Real production systems organize memory in tiers, each trading off speed of access, total capacity, and cost per token. The context window sits at the top, with progressively slower, larger, and cheaper stores below it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The analogy to operating system memory is evident. Modern agent memory systems draw heavily on the way operating systems page data between fast RAM and slower disk, promoting and demoting information as its relevance rises and falls.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A typical four-tier hierarchy starts with the context window at the top, fast and tightly bounded, with every token expensive at scale. Below it sits short-term or session memory, holding recent activity that has yet to be summarized or evicted. Beneath that is the long-term store, where persistent facts, embeddings, and structured summaries live across sessions. At the bottom is the cold archive, used for rarely-accessed material kept for audit or future reference.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" justify"><span>Information moves up and down this hierarchy as the agent works. A fact stated three sessions ago might be sitting in the long-term store, and the moment it becomes relevant, the system retrieves it and promotes it back into the context window. Conversely, when a session ends, the most useful parts of the context window get summarized and written down into the lower tiers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>ChatGPT’s memory feature uses a simple version of this idea. Stored user facts and summaries of recent conversations get prepended to every new prompt, while the current session occupies the working tier. The sophistication lies in what gets promoted to long-term memory in the first place, rather than in elaborate retrieval at read time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A hierarchy describes where memory lives. The kinds of memory we are storing are a separate question, organized along a different axis.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Types</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The field has converged on four functional categories of agent memory, drawing on concepts from cognitive science adapted for language model agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Working memory holds whatever sits in the live context window for the current task. For example, if the agent is helping us debug a function right now, the function code and our recent messages occupy working memory. The moment this task ends, working memory clears.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Episodic memory holds records of specific past interactions, anchored in time. A statement like “Three days ago, this user asked about onboarding new engineers, and we discussed checklist templates” represents an episodic memory, capturing a particular event with its context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Semantic memory stores facts and knowledge that stand independent of any specific interaction. Statements like “Adam prefers Python over JavaScript” and “his team uses GitHub Actions for CI” function as semantic memories, surviving across sessions and applying wherever they are relevant.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Procedural memory captures learned ways of doing things. If the agent has figured out that this user prefers a three-section format for status updates, that preference becomes procedural memory, and the next time a status update is requested, the agent applies the format automatically.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>These four types are orthogonal to the hierarchy from the previous section.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A piece of semantic memory might live physically in the long-term store and get pulled into the context window the moment it becomes relevant. Most production agents implement at least three of these types, with the mix depending on what the agent is built to do. A customer support agent leans heavily on episodic and semantic memory, while a coding agent leans more on procedural memory. The right blend is a design choice rather than a fixed formula.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of this still leaves one important question open.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How does the agent actually decide, on each turn, what to retrieve and place in the model’s view?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Storage can possibly be thought of as the easy half of agent memory. Writing a fact to a database or indexing a summary in a vector store are solved problems with mature tooling. The harder half is retrieval, which is the act of deciding on every new turn what belongs in the model’s awareness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Retrieval is hard because it requires judgment about relevance, and relevance shifts from one message to the next. For example, the user’s preference for Python matters when they are asking about a new project, while that same preference fades in importance when they are asking about pizza recipes. A good retrieval system surfaces relevant items at exactly the moment they are useful, and leaves the rest sitting quietly in storage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>The full loop runs on every user message.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The user sends a message, and the system retrieves relevant items from each memory tier using a mix of keyword search, semantic similarity, and recency signals. It assembles a context window in a deliberate order, often placing the most important material near the beginning and the end where the model’s attention is strongest. The model runs and returns a response, after which the system writes part of the new exchange back into memory, often as a summary, sometimes with a decay score so that importance fades over time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Consider two agents to see why retrieval matters so much.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first has a perfect database of past interactions paired with a retrieval system that frequently picks the wrong record. The second has an empty memory store and operates only on what the user tells it in the current session. The second often outperforms the first, because it understands the bounds of what it can rely on, while the first surfaces stale or irrelevant information confidently and reasons on top of it as though it were ground truth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In other words, memory failures in production are typically retrieval failures in disguise.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The memory architecture described above involves several tradeoffs that engineering teams must navigate carefully. Four stand out as particularly important:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Recency versus relevance:</span></strong><span> Do we retrieve the most recent items from memory, or the most semantically similar ones? Most systems do both, and blending them well is an ongoing engineering puzzle. Leaning too far on recency means the agent forgets useful older context, while leaning too far on relevance means the agent fixates on a strong-but-stale match.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Summarization versus fidelity:</span></strong><span> Compressing old context into summaries saves tokens, which makes everything cheaper and faster. The compression is also lossy, and the loss is uneven. Names, dates, and specific commitments get smoothed away in summarization, while general themes survive. The agent stays confident even after the precise detail has quietly disappeared.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Staleness:</span></strong><span> A fact that was true six months ago can be confidently wrong today. For example, the user who may have told the agent “I am a vegetarian” in 2024 might be eating non-vegetarian again in 2026. The memory system has only blunt heuristics for guessing that the world has moved on, so it keeps serving the old fact with full confidence. Staleness in high-relevance memories remains an open research problem.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Memory poisoning:</span></strong><span> Long-term memory is also a long-term attack surface. A subtly malicious instruction written into the store six months ago will sit there influencing every retrieval until somebody notices. The same property that makes memory useful, persistence, also makes it dangerous when the contents are wrong or hostile.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A memory system makes sense when the agent needs continuity across sessions or runs long-horizon tasks where context compounds. For one-shot tasks, it adds complexity beyond what the task requires.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Five core ideas from this article are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model is stateless. Every API call begins from a fresh slate, and any continuity we observe is the work of the surrounding system rather than the model itself.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The context window is the model’s only surface of awareness. Writing everything into it fails for reasons of cost, latency, and degraded attention in long prompts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Real systems organize memory in a hierarchy of tiers, with the context window at the top and progressively slower, larger, cheaper stores below it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Different kinds of information call for different kinds of memory, with working, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory each serving a distinct purpose.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The main engineering problem in this area is retrieval, which is the question of what deserves to enter the model’s awareness on each new turn, with tradeoffs around staleness, summarization loss, and security.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The practical takeaway from all of this is simple.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The next time we see a product feature labeled “memory” or read about an agent that “remembers across sessions,” the right question moves away from “can the model remember this?” and toward “what does the memory architecture around this model actually do, and what tradeoffs has it accepted?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li item.title: p99 0ms autocomplete for 240 million domain names
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
p99 0ms autocomplete for 240 million domain names

Ruurtjan Pul

6 minutes by Ruurtjan Pul Wirewiki's autocomplete feels instant by fetching suggestions on keydown, before the user finishes pressing a key. The server uses an in-memory trie for popular domains and a compressed disk index for the rest, responding in under 15ms for 99% of requests. The main remaining bottleneck is network distance, since a single European server adds too much latency for users further away. Multiple geo-distributed servers would fix this but are hard to justify for a niche tool.
item.description: p99 0ms autocomplete for 240 million domain names

item.title: The cost YAGNI was never about
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The cost YAGNI was never about

Kent Beck

4 minutes by Kent Beck YAGNI means build things when you need them, not before. Building too early costs you twice: you lose the ability to make better choices once you have real information, and you spend money before you earn it back. AI tools make it tempting to build speculative structure for free, but that makes the problem worse, not better. The cost was never in the typing.
item.description: The cost YAGNI was never about

item.title: A story of delayed AWS pipelines
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A story of delayed AWS pipelines

Vladimir Romashov

7 minutes by Vladimir Romashov A single Terraform data source for AWS organization info secretly makes three API calls, not one. These calls share a rate limit across an entire AWS organization, so dozens of teams running pipelines at once exhaust that limit fast. This caused roughly 1 in 10 pipelines to stall for up to 15 minutes. A fix now shipped in terraform-provider-aws v6.29.0 makes the extra calls optional.
item.description: A story of delayed AWS pipelines

item.title: How LLMs actually work
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How LLMs actually work

0xkato

23 minutes by 0xkato Large language models turn text into integers, look up learned vectors for each, then pass everything through many stacked layers. Each layer lets tokens share information through attention, then processes each token independently through a feed-forward network. Residual connections and normalization keep deep stacks stable and trainable. The model ends by scoring every possible next token and repeating the process one step at a time.
item.description: How LLMs actually work

item.title: curl and CVE dispute
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
curl and CVE dispute

Daniel Stenberg

7 minutes by Daniel Stenberg The curl project became a CVE Numbering Authority, giving it full control over assigning CVE identifiers to its own security issues. Not every bug deserves a CVE, and curl deliberately skips them for issues so unlikely that raising an alarm would waste effort across the industry. A reporter recently disputed this approach over a wildcard certificate hostname bug, escalating to MITRE. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: curl and CVE dispute

item.title: How to insert-or-update without headache
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to insert-or-update without headache

Chris Woodruff

EF Core has no built-in upsert, and the common workaround of checking then writing causes one database round-trip per record, which collapses under large payloads. Raw T-SQL MERGE with a table-valued parameter solves this for SQL Server in a single atomic call, but requires hand-written SQL tied to one provider. Entity Framework Extensions fills the gap with BulkMerge, which handles inserts and updates in one call across all major databases, though always set a business key as the match column or every record silently inserts as new.
item.description: How to insert-or-update without headache

item.title: Strongly typed generic object in C#
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Strongly typed generic object in C#

Jiří Činčura

A generic class is built step by step to add type safety in C#. A self-referencing type constraint is added, then a non-null constraint on top. The result is clean but serves no real purpose.
item.description: Strongly typed generic object in C#

item.title: Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core

Mukesh Murugan

ASP.NET Core has one authorization system: policies. Role and claim checks are just shortcuts that compile down to the same pipeline. A policy bundles requirements together using AND logic, while multiple handlers for one requirement use OR logic. Handlers run with full dependency injection, so rules can check databases, clocks, or external services. Set a fallback policy on every new API so forgotten endpoints fail closed instead of open.
item.description: Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Avoiding ToString allocations with StringBuilder.MoveChunks
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Avoiding ToString allocations with StringBuilder.MoveChunks

Andrew Lock

In this post I take a short look at the new StringBuilder.MoveChunks API introduced in .NET 11 preview 5. First we'll described what the API does and how to use it, then we'll look at how it's implemented. Finally, we'll look at why this API was introduced.
item.description: Avoiding ToString allocations with StringBuilder.MoveChunks

item.title: The case of the empty IIS deployment
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The case of the empty IIS deployment

Barret Blake

A version mismatch between packages in a large .NET solution caused dotnet publish to silently generate an empty package. Because the conflict only triggers a warning rather than an error, the build pipeline showed green while deploying nothing. The fix was aligning package versions across projects, with plans to treat that specific warning as an error and add a deployment check to catch empty packages before they ship. And the most popular article from the last issue was: * Outbox pattern in .NET: How to implement reliable message
item.description: The case of the empty IIS deployment

RAG</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The query is converted into an embedding and matched against a vector database.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The top-K closest chunks are pulled out and passed to the LLM as context. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM writes a grounded answer using only what was retrieved.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Graph RAG</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The query is classified: specific questions route to local search, broad questions route to global search.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Local search: query embedded → vector DB finds matching entities → pipeline traverses across the knowledge graph collecting linked context → LLM synthesis final answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Global search: no vector search, no graph traversal → community reports loaded in batches → LLM scores each for relevance → top-ranked context → LLM synthesizes final response.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Agentic RAG</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A reasoning agent reads the query, breaks it into sub-questions and picks the sources.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The context across multiple sources is retrieved, depending on the sub-query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Another agent checks whether the retrieved context answers the question. If not, it re-retrieves.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Once satisfied, the final answer is synthesized by LLM based on the prompt.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Standard RAG is fast and cheap but if the wrong chunk is retrieved, the answer is wrong and nothing catches it.Use it when the answer lives in your documents and speed matters. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Graph RAG is expensive to build and slow to update. Use it for structured knowledge like legal, compliance, or biomedical data. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>Agentic RAG is more capable and flexible but slower, expensive, and harder to debug. Use it when the question needs multi-step reasoning and self-correction. </span><br><span>Over to you: Which of these are you running in production?</span></span></p><div style="font-size: style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Strings store one value per key. They work for counters, session tokens, and cached payloads.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Hashes store an object's fields under one key. You can update one field without rewriting the rest.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lists are ordered sequences with fast push and pop at both ends. They fit queues, feeds, and recent-item lists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sets hold unique members and support intersection, union, and difference. They cover tagging, follower overlap, and deduplication.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sorted Sets rank members by a numeric score. They handle leaderboards, priority queues, and top-N or range-by-score queries.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Streams are an append-only log with consumer groups. Each consumer tracks its own position, and the server tracks unacknowledged messages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>JSON stores nested documents with JSONPath access. You can update a field deep in a document without read-modify-write.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Geospatial provides latitude/longitude indexes with radius and box queries. Under the hood it's a Sorted Set with geohash scores.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Vector Set runs approximate nearest-neighbor search over embeddings. It's the retrieval step in most RAG pipelines.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Time Series stores timestamped samples with built-in retention, downsampling, and labels. It fits metrics, telemetry, and IoT data.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over to you: All ten are built-in as of Redis 8. Which one do you use most outside of caching?</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>API Security Best Practices</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most API breaches happen because of broken authorization, leaked secrets, or missing rate limits. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Use Modern OAuth/OIDC + MFA: PKCE for public clients, short-lived tokens, and step-up MFA for anything sensitive. Implicit and password grants should be dead by now.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Enforce Fine-Grained Authorization: Check object, function, and field-level permissions on every request. BOLA is still the top API vulnerability.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Minimize Scopes and Data: Give each client the smallest token scope and the least data it needs. Only return the fields the caller actually needs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Encrypt Every Hop: TLS for external traffic and mTLS between services. If it crosses a network boundary, encrypt it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Protect Secrets and Keys: Store signing keys in HSM-backed vaults. Rotate them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Validate Requests with Schemas: Reject unknown fields, oversized payloads, and suspicious URLs at the gateway. Don't let bad input reach your business logic.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Rate Limit and Cap Resources: Quotas per user, payload size caps, and execution timeouts. Without these, one misbehaving client takes down your entire system.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Defend Sensitive Business Flows: Protect login, checkout, and OTP with anti-bot, idempotency keys, and step-up auth.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Control Outbound and Third-Party Calls: Allowlist where your API can call out to and block internal metadata endpoints. Your security is only as strong as your weakest integration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Harden Config and Error Handling: Deny by default on CORS, methods, and debug endpoints. Return generic errors, never stack traces.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Inventory APIs and Versions: Track every endpoint, version, and shadow API. You can't secure what you don't know exists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Log, Detect, and Respond: Push auth decisions and anomalies to a SIEM. Alert on 401 spikes before they become incidents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over to you: Which of these best practices is the hardest to enforce across your services?</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: The Testing Pyramid is a widely accepted strategy for structuring tests into three key layers:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Unit Tests: These are the foundation of the pyramid. Unit tests are fast, isolated, and low-cost to write and maintain. They test individual functions, methods, or components.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Integration Tests: These tests validate interactions between components, such as APIs, databases, and external services. They are slower than unit tests and require more setup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>E2E Tests: These simulate real user flows from start to finish across the full system. They are expensive to write and maintain and tend to be slow to execute.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you go up the pyramid, the cost of test development, execution, and maintenance increases. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over to you: item.title: Riding Technology Waves
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Riding Technology Waves

“A lot of senior leaders, even “leaders” at tech companies, are fundamentally insecure about technology. They’re either not technical by training or so out of practice that they don’t know how their products work. This is especially true in fields where projecting confidence is a key part of the job: Sales, Marketing, Human Resources, and arguably even Security are all examples.”

#Leadership CareerGrowth
item.description: Riding Technology Waves

item.title: Who Will Be The Senior Engineers Of 2035?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Who Will Be The Senior Engineers Of 2035?

James Stanier

“We’ll start by looking at the pipeline we used to have: how senior engineers traditionally emerged through years of mistakes, mentorship, and low-stakes learning. Then we’ll examine what’s replacing it, and hypothesise whether AI will actually fill the gap. We’ll explore three possible scenarios for 2035, and finish with what this means depending on where you sit in the industry.”

#Leadership Management CareerGrowth
item.description: Who Will Be The Senior Engineers Of 2035?

item.title: What Being “Inspiring" Actually Means
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
What Being “Inspiring" Actually Means

Wes Kao

“Being inspiring is not about how passionate your delivery is. You don’t have to get up in front of everyone, or try to cosplay what a bold leader sounds like. You can sound like yourself. Perhaps the most articulate and clear-eyed version of yourself, but still yourself.”

#Leadership Communication
item.description: What Being “Inspiring" Actually Means

item.title: 5 Lessons At 50
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
5 Lessons At 50

Murat Demirbas

(1) Caution is warranted. (2) Realism helps you understand how the world runs (3) Competence is bliss (4) Do what you like (5). Your attitude determines your success.

#CareerGrowth Wellbeing
item.description: 5 Lessons At 50

item.title: Find A New Role - Worksheet
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Find A New Role - Worksheet

Lara Hogan

Lara built a worksheet to help you identify: what do I want in a new role? How can I make sure I find the right place? Where do I even start?

#CareerGrowth Guide
item.description: Find A New Role - Worksheet

item.title: Loop Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Loop Engineering

Addy Osmani

“Loop engineering is replacing yourself as the person who prompts the agent. You design the system that does it instead. A loop here can be thought of a recursive goal where you define a purpose and the AI iterates until complete. It’s roughly five building blocks and Claude Code and Codex both have all five now.”

#AI Architecture Agents
item.description: Loop Engineering

item.title: I Stored A Website In A Favicon
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
I Stored A Website In A Favicon

Tim Wehrle

“Every website has a favicon. It's that little icon in your browser tab. Usually you upload it once and then never think about it again. But. A favicon is just an image. An image is just pixels. And pixels are just bytes. So of course I wondered if I could store something inside one.”

#Entertaining
item.description: I Stored A Website In A Favicon

16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A service architecture can end up slower to change, harder to operate, and less reliable than the single large system it replaced, and it can cost more to run while doing it. This is rarely the work of a careless team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How many decisions does it take to reach that point?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It rarely takes a single bad one. The path to such a situation is built from individually sound choices, a clean separation here, an independent deployment there, a new service each time a part of the system felt distinct enough to stand on its own. Those reasonable steps accumulate into an arrangement no one would have chosen on purpose, and the problems that emerge look like a catalog of separate mistakes even though nearly all of them trace back to one early decision about how to break a system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>At a basic level, a service is a part of a system that can be deployed on its own and controls its own data. This means it does not reach into any other service’s database to do its work. It also talks to other services over a network. Inside a single program, one function calling another takes a few nanoseconds and either returns an answer or raises an error. The same call across a service boundary can take a few milliseconds, and it can also time out or succeed halfway and leave things in an odd state. Almost every anti-pattern below emerges from this one problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at some of the most important anti-patterns in service architecture, how they happen, and how they can be avoided.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Same with Sentry’s MCP server. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1af92e6-4aa3-426f-88e7-cb1ecff7c563?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Check out Sentry</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd917f63-93b6-4e9a-a404-7faa418c11f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Google Cloud Run</span></a></strong><span> – a fully managed platform that runs your code directly on top of Google’s scalable infrastructure. Oh, it has automatic zonal failover out of the box – something that Coinbase </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c336b85c-a732-49f2-854d-6f9b9100fe1f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>could have used</span></a><span> a few weeks back! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd917f63-93b6-4e9a-a404-7faa418c11f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Get started</span></a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Navdeep Singh – oftentimes better known as NeetCode – is the creator of NeetCode.io, one of the most popular coding interview preparation platforms and YouTube channels for software engineers. Before building NeetCode full-time, he worked as a software engineer at Amazon and Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer, I sit down with Neet to discuss his path from Amazon and Google to building his own startup, why he left Amazon after just two months, what he learned at Google, and the decision to leave a stable engineering career to bet on himself. We also discuss what coding interview preparation teaches beyond passing interviews, the value of going deep on difficult problems, and why systems thinking and domain expertise remain essential engineering skills in the age of AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Throughout the conversation, NeetCode makes the case that learning hard things is one of the </span><em><span>single best </span></em><span>investments an engineer can make, helping build the judgment and expertise that remain valuable no matter how the tools change.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Key observations from Neet</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are 10 interesting takeaways from our chat:</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/babf106b-3932-4b72-b8c4-f1b91c23a25f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/xafwfGVBxos" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Companies have no real method for evaluating engineers, and likely never did</span></strong><span>. Neet believes that the leetcode-style interview survived not because it predicts job performance but because it scales suprisingly well at large tech companies that need to train hundreds (or thousands!) of interviewers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. The CAP theorem’s “two of three” framing is widely taught but technically shaky.</span></strong><span> Neet felt that is an awkward theorem that is incomplete, and felt validated when Martin Kleppmann </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c40d5049-d1e0-4dd3-bde3-13dac2d90946?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>publicly criticized it too</span></a><span>. This is a good reminder that it’s worth thinking for yourself, and not accepting theorems as true, without understanding them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Amazon’s intense culture left Neet in afraid to ask for help – and that paradoxically, this helped him at Google.</span></strong><span> At Neet’s first job, he became used to work alone and to never ask questions, and continued this working style at Google. At Gooogle, his Google manager read him as independent: and thanks to this independence, he got promoted very quickly from L3 to L4 (to the mid-level engineering role.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. The Neetcode YouTube channel took off after Neet posted that he’ll post less because he got into Google. </span></strong><span>Before he shared that he got a software engieneering job at Google – back at that time, one of the most competitive companies to get into – there were not many people watching the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e678c52a-de11-42f1-a066-25bbcf74e924?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Neetcode channel</span></a><span>. Sharing that he got into Google turned out to be the best “sales pitch” though: and suddenly, people wanted to understand what he’d practiced that helped him get this job!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Cheating tools are resulting in in-person whiteboard interviews returning at Google. </span></strong><span>Neet noted how Google has started to return to onside onsite coding interviews, because it is only in this setting that interviewiewers can make sure that interviewees are not using invisible AI-powered cheating tools, which make it effortless to do well on data structure and algorithms (DSA) interviews.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Neet finds AI most valuable as a tech-debt and refactoring assistant. </span></strong><span>Neet is using AI to clean up years of very bad code quality on the Neetcode backend. Doint so also validates his original decision to take shortcuts because they could later be corrected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Effort is becoming the differentiator because AI made everything else cheap.</span></strong><span> Neet says how you can prompt a design, a feature, or an answer (to a coding question.) But you cannot prompt caring, or your ability to defend </span><em><span>why</span></em><span> you made a choice. You can only do these if you put in the effort, and don’t leave it all to AI!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Predictions of coding’s death haven’t materialized as expected. </span></strong><span>Despite dramatic AI model improvements, Neet does not observe most engineers aren’t being laid off. In fact, he sees the opposite: devs doing more work than before!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Weighing tradeoffs is likely to be someting that we’ll remain better than LLMs. </span></strong><span>While LLMs have become a lot better at coding, Neet doesn’t believe they will be all that helpful making decisions involving judgement tradeoffs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. When hiring for Neetcode, personality traits and motivation are more important than coding skill. </span></strong><span>Neet’s best, recent hire is still an undergrad. This hire does not have as much coding experience, but does exceptionally well thanks to high agency. As Neet explained: “even if they have no idea how to start it, a week later they’ll have learned everything about it.”</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Apple’s most ambitious AI feature runs in about a gigabyte of memory on the iPhone. The same company runs a much larger model on its own cloud servers, and the two diverge in almost every architectural choice beyond the word “transformer” in their lineage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The same split shows up at Google, Microsoft, and Meta, where one family of small models targets devices and a different family of large models targets data centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Small and large language models are different engineering responses to different constraints, and the differences begin with where each model runs, what hardware it targets, and how it was trained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will explore those constraints through three layers of model design, look at the tradeoffs that come with each approach, and investigate the production systems that combine both small and large models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Foundations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Before we look at what makes the two classes different, it helps to be precise about what makes them the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both small and large language models are transformer-based decoder models, built by stacking layers of the same basic computational block. Each block runs an attention operation, which figures out which previous tokens matter most for predicting the next one, followed by a feed-forward computation that mixes that information through a wide intermediate layer. The model repeats this block thirty or more times before producing a probability distribution over what the next token should be.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>Both classes go through similar training stages. They start with pretraining on large text corpora, where the model learns to predict the next token across billions of examples. They typically follow with supervised fine-tuning on specific instruction patterns, and many go through reinforcement learning from human feedback, which shapes how the model handles ambiguity and stays helpful in conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The size of a model refers to its number of parameters, which are the learned weights adjusted during training. A small model in 2026 typically has between half a billion and fourteen billion parameters. A large model has tens of billions to hundreds of billions of parameters, and sometimes more.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Constraints</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Three constraints pull the designs of small and large models in opposite directions.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Deployment target:</span></strong><span> Where the model runs determines its memory, battery, and latency budgets.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Inference economics:</span></strong><span> Training is paid once, but serving is paid per request, which inverts the math at scale.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Training budget:</span></strong><span> Smaller budgets push teams toward efficiency through data quality and distillation rather than raw scale.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The deployment target determines everything that follows.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A model that runs on a phone has a memory budget measured in single gigabytes, a battery budget measured in milliamps, and a latency budget measured in milliseconds. A model that runs in a data center operates in a more permissive environment, with concerns around throughput, batching efficiency, and cost per request, but with an absolute resource ceiling orders of magnitude higher.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Inference economics is the second pressure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Training a model is a one-time cost paid at the start of its life, while serving the model is a recurring cost paid every time someone uses it. For a high-volume product, the inference bill quickly dwarfs the training bill, so a team designing for high inference volume will gladly spend more training compute upfront to save inference compute across billions of requests downstream.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The training budget is the third pressure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A frontier large model can cost tens of millions of dollars to train, while most teams working on small models operate with a small fraction of that, and the smaller budget forces choices. Those teams have to find other levers beyond raw scale, which usually means smarter training data, distillation from larger teachers, and more efficient training recipes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These three constraints reinforce each other rather than acting in isolation. A model designed for the phone has a small inference budget per request and usually a smaller training budget too, while a model designed for the data center has the opposite profile across all three axes. The result is two distinct design regions in the same space.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI
