optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Architecture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The architecture differences begin with a quick observation about inference.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>During generation, the model has to keep around the keys and values for every previous token, since attention works by comparing the current token against all earlier ones. This stored set is called the KV cache, and it grows linearly with the length of the conversation. For long generations, the cache often dominates memory bandwidth and storage, more than the parameters themselves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This single fact decides how small-model architectures get designed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In the original transformer design, every attention head has its own keys and values, an arrangement called multi-head attention. For long sequences, the resulting cache footprint grows large enough to dominate the model’s memory consumption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Grouped-query attention attacks the problem directly. The number of query heads stays the same, but several queries share a single key-value pair. A model with thirty-two query heads might use only eight key-value groups, which cuts the cache footprint by a factor of four with minimal quality loss. Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and most modern small models use grouped-query attention by default, and many large models have adopted it as well because the math also helps at scale.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some small models push further. Gemma 2 interleaves sliding window attention with full attention across layers, so some layers attend only to the most recent few thousand tokens rather than the full context. This trades a bit of long-range reasoning for a significantly smaller cache. Apple’s on-device model shares its KV cache across multiple decoder layers, reusing the same stored state in several places.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>These architectural decisions all serve the same goal of shrinking the runtime cost of inference, which is the constraint that matters most when the model has to run on a device with a few gigabytes of memory to spare.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Training</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Two models with identical architectures can end up with very different capabilities depending on what they were trained on and how.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Three techniques define the current state of the art in small-model training:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Data curation:</span></strong><span> Carefully chosen and synthetically generated training data can substitute for raw volume.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Knowledge distillation:</span></strong><span> A smaller student model learns from a larger teacher model’s output distribution.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Overtraining:</span></strong><span> Modern small models see far more training tokens than compute-optimal ratios suggest, trading training cost for inference savings.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first technique is data curation. In 2023, a Microsoft research team published a paper called “Textbooks Are All You Need.” They trained a 1.3 billion parameter coding model on roughly seven billion tokens of carefully filtered code and synthetically generated textbook-style data. The model matched or beat models trained on hundreds of billions of tokens of raw web scrape. Training data quality could substitute for training data volume, at least for certain capabilities. The Phi family kept building on that insight, and the modern Phi-4 model continues to lean heavily on synthetic data quality as its primary lever.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The second technique is knowledge distillation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The small model, called the student, learns from a larger model, called the teacher, by mimicking the teacher’s output distribution rather than only learning from raw text. The richer training signal helps the student pick up patterns it would struggle to learn from the underlying corpus alone. Gemma 2 used this approach to train its nine billion parameter model, while training its twenty-seven billion parameter version from scratch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The third technique is overtraining relative to compute-optimal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In 2022, the Chinchilla paper from DeepMind established that for a fixed compute budget, the best model came from balancing parameter count and training data, roughly twenty tokens of training data per parameter. Modern small models deliberately train on far more data than that ratio suggests. A three-billion-parameter model might see many trillions of tokens during training, which is many times the Chinchilla-optimal amount. Once the model gets deployed, every percentage point of quality improvement saves inference compute across billions of requests, so the team spends more on training to save more on serving.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Deployment</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The final layer of design choices covers how the model executes on real hardware. The two dominant techniques are quantization, which shrinks the storage cost of each parameter, and KV cache management, which shrinks the runtime cost of generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Quantization is the practice of storing each parameter with fewer bits. A standard pretrained model stores each parameter as a sixteen-bit floating point number, where cutting that to eight bits halves the memory footprint and cutting to four bits halves it again. The post-training approach is faster to implement but tends to lose quality at aggressive bit widths, while quantization-aware training preserves quality at the cost of more complex training.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" justify"><span>Hardware mapping is the next consideration. Apple’s Neural Engine has different strengths from an NVIDIA Jetson, which has different strengths from a data center H100, and the model design follows the target hardware. Phi-4-mini gets tuned for consumer GPUs. Gemma 3 4B variants run on NVIDIA Jetson Orin for edge AI deployments in robotics and embedded systems. Apple’s 3B model runs on the iPhone’s Neural Engine with the assumption that the device also handles other workloads at the same time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>KV cache management is the second major lever, and it connects directly back to the architecture section. The cache stores keys and values for every previous token during generation, and its size determines how much memory the model utilizes at runtime. Grouped-query attention attacks this by reducing the number of key-value heads, and Apple’s on-device model goes further by sharing its cache across multiple decoder layers.</span></p><div justify"><span>These deployment decisions stack on top of everything earlier. The same architectural choices that shrink the KV cache also make quantization easier, and the same training recipes that produce capable small models also produce models that survive aggressive compression.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Small models perform well on standard benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval. Production usage looks more varied. Three gaps tend to matter most:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Generalization gap:</span></strong><span> Small models are more brittle outside their training distribution.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Reasoning gap:</span></strong><span> Multi-step problems still favor larger models, though the gap is closing.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Knowledge ceiling:</span></strong><span> Parameters function as memory, so small models have a hard cap on what they can store.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first gap is generalization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Small models tend to be more brittle outside their training distribution, and they can be excellent at tasks similar to what they saw during training, while showing weakness on unexpected ones. A small model trained heavily on code performs well on code but may struggle with creative writing in an unusual style. A model trained on synthetic textbook data does well on textbook-style questions but can falter on the messy, ambiguous prompts that real users send.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The second gap is multi-step reasoning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For problems that require chaining inference across many tokens, large models still have a noticeable advantage. The gap has been closing thanks to step-by-step reasoning techniques and reasoning-focused fine-tuning, but at very small parameter counts, the ceiling remains real. Phi-4 has done well on math reasoning specifically because Microsoft optimized for that capability through training data design, while a general-purpose small model usually shows a clearer gap.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The third gap is world knowledge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Parameters function as a form of memory, and a larger model can store more facts, more named entities, more obscure references, and more multilingual coverage. A small model has a fundamental cap on how much it can know, since storage requires parameters and parameters require memory. For applications that need broad factual recall, the small model often pairs with an external knowledge source that the model queries when needed, since trying to fit all that knowledge into the parameters themselves would push the model past its budget.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Hybrids</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most interesting design question in 2026 is rarely which model to use. The more useful question is how to compose multiple models into a system that uses each for what it does best. Three patterns appear in most production setups.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Routing:</span></strong><span> A small model handles requests directly and escalates harder ones to a large model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Guardrails:</span></strong><span> A small model filters input or output around the large model’s core work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Drafting:</span></strong><span> A small fast model generates candidate tokens that a larger model verifies in a batch.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most common pattern is routing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A small model handles the request directly if it falls within its competence, and escalates to a large model when the request is harder than it can confidently handle. The pattern resembles caching tiers in a distributed system, where the fast, cheap layer handles the common case, and the slower, more expensive layer handles the rest. The router itself is often a small classifier model that decides which path to take.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The second pattern is the guardrail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A small model sits in front of the large model to filter or classify input before the expensive computation runs, checking for unsafe content, classifying the intent of the request, or stripping out information that should stay private. A second small model often sits on the output side, doing similar checks before the response gets returned to the user. These guardrail models are cheap, fast, and specialized, which makes them well-suited to the role.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The third pattern is the drafter, sometimes called speculative decoding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A small fast model generates candidate tokens, and a larger, more capable model verifies them in batch. When the verifications agree, the system gets the throughput of the small model with the quality of the large one. Apple’s on-device system uses a draft model alongside its base model for exactly this reason. The technique sounds like a hack, but it has become standard in production inference systems.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Picking a model class is the wrong frame for most product decisions. Designing a system around multiple model classes is the right frame, and the interesting design work lives in the composition layer, the routing logic, the fallback behavior, and the orchestration between models.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The question we started with was “small versus large language models,” and the more useful version of that question turns out to be “which constraints drove each model’s design.” The size of a model is a downstream consequence of those constraints rather than the starting point for the design.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Three layers of design choices flow from the constraints:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Architecture adapts through attention variants like grouped-query and sliding-window attention that shrink the KV cache.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Training adapts through high-quality synthetic data, distillation from larger teachers, and deliberate overtraining relative to compute-optimal ratios.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Deployment adapts through quantization, KV cache management, and careful hardware mapping. Each layer reinforces the others, and the result is two distinct design regions in the same space.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Small models are extremely capable for their size, and they have a real ceiling on generalization, on multi-step reasoning, and on broad world knowledge. Production systems handle this by composing both classes, using small models for the common case and large models for the harder requests, sometimes with multiple small models acting as routers, guardrails, and drafters around a larger core.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For a working engineer choosing between models, the right starting point is the constraints rather than the benchmark. The questions that matter are about deployment target, inference budget, and the shape of the request distribution in production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin: 8px 0;"><span>Use the code </span><strong>SCOOP</strong></p></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom companies are not short on AI ambition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Across the industry, operators are talking about autonomous networks, AI-powered customer experience, predictive maintenance, energy optimization, fraud detection, AI-RAN, edge AI, and eventually 6G networks that are intelligent by design.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The vision is exciting. Instead of networks that mostly react to problems, telcos want networks that can sense what is happening, predict what might go wrong, recommend the best action, and eventually fix issues with little or no human intervention.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That sounds powerful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But there is one uncomfortable problem hiding under all of this momentum: AI cannot do any of that if the data behind it is fragmented, delayed, ungoverned, or difficult to access.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is where telecom’s AI story gets complicated.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos are some of the most data-rich companies in the world. Every call, text, app session, roaming event, dropped connection, device movement, network fault, billing interaction, and customer complaint leaves a trail of information. The network is constantly producing signals.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But having a lot of data is not the same as being ready for AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For AI to work inside telecom operations, the data has to be available when needed. It has to be clean enough to trust. It has to be governed properly. It has to be connected across different systems. And in many cases, it has to be available in real time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is the real challenge.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Telco AI is moving from “nice to have” to network-critical</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the early stages, a lot of AI in telecom focused on safer use cases. Think customer service chatbots, sales support, marketing personalization, or back-office automation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Those still matter. But the industry is now moving toward a much bigger goal: using AI inside the network itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That includes things like predicting equipment failures before they happen, detecting congestion, optimizing energy use, improving service quality, identifying fraud, troubleshooting outages, and supporting autonomous network operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a different level of responsibility.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If an AI tool summarizes a customer support ticket incorrectly, that is a problem. But if an AI system makes a bad recommendation inside a live network environment, the consequences can be much bigger. It could affect service reliability, enterprise customers, emergency communications, regulatory compliance, or customer trust.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is why telco AI needs a stronger foundation than ordinary enterprise AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It cannot simply rely on models that look smart in a demo. It needs trusted operational data, clear governance, strong guardrails, and real-time context.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">The problem is not that telcos lack data</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The funny thing is, telecom does not have a data shortage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It has almost the opposite problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos have massive amounts of data sitting across radio access networks, core networks, transport networks, OSS and BSS platforms, billing systems, customer care systems, cybersecurity tools, edge environments, and cloud platforms.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem is that this data often lives in separate systems that were never designed to work together easily.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some data is owned by network teams. Some sits with customer experience teams. Some is locked inside vendor-specific systems. Some is stored in legacy platforms. Some is too sensitive to move freely. Some is real-time, while some is only available after delays.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So when a telco says it wants AI to improve network operations, the first question should not be, “Which model should we use?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The better question is, “Can the model actually access the right data, at the right time, with the right context and permission?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In many cases, that is where the difficulty begins.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A predictive maintenance model may need equipment data, historical fault records, weather patterns, power usage, site information, and customer complaints. But if those datasets are scattered across different systems, the model may only see part of the picture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A customer service AI may be able to answer billing questions, but if it cannot see live network conditions, it may fail to explain why a customer is experiencing slow service.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An AI system may detect an anomaly, but if it cannot connect that anomaly to customer impact, service-level agreements, or recent configuration changes, it may not know what the problem actually means.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is why fragmented data leads to shallow AI.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Real-time data changes everything</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For many industries, using yesterday’s data is good enough.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom is different.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Networks change constantly. Traffic moves. Devices roam. Cells become congested. Equipment fails. Demand spikes. Latency changes. Security threats appear. Customers complain in real time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If AI is going to support network operations, it cannot rely only on old reports. It needs a live or near-live understanding of what is happening.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is especially important for autonomous networks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An autonomous network is not just a network with dashboards. It is a network that can observe conditions, interpret what is happening, and take or recommend action. For that to work, AI needs fresh data from across the network.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why the industry is talking more about network digital twins, graph-based network views, edge inference, and real-time analytics.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A network digital twin, for example, gives operators a live or near-live representation of the network. Instead of looking at isolated metrics, teams can see how different parts of the network relate to each other. If something breaks, AI can use that connected view to help understand the root cause faster.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is powerful, but it only works when the data is accurate, current, and connected.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Without that, a digital twin becomes just another fancy map.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Governance is what makes AI trustworthy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is another piece that does not always get enough attention: governance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In telecom, governance is not just a legal or compliance checklist. It is part of the technical architecture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If an AI system is helping make network decisions, operators need to know where the data came from, who has access to it, how it was used, whether it is accurate, and what the AI is allowed to do with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This matters because telecom data can be highly sensitive. It can involve subscriber information, location-related data, enterprise traffic, infrastructure data, and operational security signals.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos cannot treat this casually.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A model that touches customer data needs privacy controls. A model that touches network operations needs audit trails. A model that recommends network actions needs policy boundaries. A model that operates across regions needs to respect data residency and sovereignty rules.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And if something goes wrong, the operator needs to answer very practical questions.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">What data did the model use?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Why did it make that recommendation?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Who approved the action?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Can we reverse it?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Was the data corrupted?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Did the model drift?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Was the policy followed?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If those questions cannot be answered, trust breaks down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And when trust breaks down, AI does not scale.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Engineers will not rely on automation they cannot explain. Regulators will not accept systems that cannot be audited. Business leaders will not keep funding pilots that cannot move safely into production.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Why many telco AI pilots get stuck</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why telecom AI often looks promising in pilot mode but becomes difficult in real operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A pilot can be controlled. The dataset can be cleaned in advance. The use case can be narrow. The environment can be simplified. The team can manually work around missing data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Production is different.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In production, the AI system has to deal with messy data, changing network conditions, multiple vendors, real customers, real outages, privacy rules, security risks, and operational accountability.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is where the cracks show.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The model works in one region but fails in another.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The AI tool identifies a fault but cannot explain the business impact.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The system recommends an action, but engineers do not trust it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The chatbot gives a customer a generic answer because it cannot access real-time network status.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The analytics team builds something impressive, but the operations team cannot deploy it safely.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These are not just AI problems. They are data readiness problems.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Telcos need a stronger data foundation</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If telecom companies want AI to move beyond pilots, they need to treat data as core network infrastructure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That means building a foundation where data is not just stored, but made usable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos need to know what data they have, where it lives, who owns it, how clean it is, how sensitive it is, and which AI systems are allowed to use it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They need data catalogs, lineage, quality checks, access controls, streaming pipelines, and common data models. They need to connect network data with customer data, service data, infrastructure data, and business context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They also need hybrid AI architectures.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Not every telco AI workload belongs in the public cloud. Some workloads need to stay close to the network because of latency, cost, privacy, or regulatory concerns. Others can run in private cloud, edge environments, or on-prem systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The future will likely be hybrid. AI will need to run wherever the data and operational requirements make the most sense.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In simple terms: telcos need to bring AI closer to the data, not always force the data to move toward AI.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">The winners will be the operators that make data usable</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The telcos that solve this first will have a real advantage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They will be able to use AI to detect issues earlier, reduce downtime, lower energy consumption, improve customer experience, speed up troubleshooting, and create new enterprise services around edge AI and secure connectivity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They will also be better positioned for the shift toward 6G, where intelligence is expected to become more deeply embedded into the network itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But operators that do not fix their data foundation may face a different reality.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They may continue announcing AI strategies, launching pilots, and testing new tools, but struggle to turn those projects into daily operational value. Over time, the gap between AI-ready telcos and data-fragmented telcos will become harder to close.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is the real risk.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The future of telecom AI will not be decided only by who has the most models, the biggest budget, or the strongest vendor partnerships.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It will be decided by who has the cleanest, most accessible, most governed, and most real-time data foundation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Bottom line</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom AI is not failing because the industry lacks ambition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The ambition is clearly there.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The real risk is that telcos are trying to build intelligent networks on top of disconnected data systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">AI cannot optimize a network it cannot fully see. It cannot automate decisions if the data is delayed. It cannot be trusted if the data is ungoverned. And it cannot scale if every use case requires teams to manually stitch together information from different systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For telcos, governed real-time data is no longer a back-office concern. It is becoming the foundation of AI-native operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Without it, telecom AI will remain a collection of promising pilots.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">With it, telcos have a real shot at building networks that are not only faster and more efficient, but intelligent enough to adapt, recover, and improve in real time.</p><div class="callout-block" data-callout="true" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;background-color: rgb(238,238,238);border-radius: 8px;margin: 32px 0;padding: 16px 32px;margin-bottom: 0;"><h2 style="font-family: 'SF Pro 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’m obviously biased because I started coding almost 30 years ago and built decades of muscle memory on top of a terminal-centric workflow ever since. But I did try GUIs every once in a while, from Visual Basic, Visual Studio, to Atom, and now the latest Codex app.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reason I stick with terminals is very simple. I keep my flow and focus best when my hands never leave the keyboard. Some GUIs let you do everything via keyboard shortcuts as well, but they’re very inconsistent about it, which makes it hard to build strong muscle memory.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Terminal Emulator</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The terminal emulator I’ve been using for many years is</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d28a4770-7603-4696-9509-4b813cc0d634?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> WezTerm</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It’s the only terminal I’ve found that is highly performant, customizable, and works consistently even when I’m forced to use Windows. 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The CLI agent harnesses nowadays are quite commoditized, and you won’t really go wrong with any of them. Almost everything I share below works with any mainstream harness you can find.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In fact, I actually recommend avoiding the “fancy” gimmicks that only some agents have, such as auto-managed memory. They’re often designed to lock you into a particular vendor, when in reality you benefit a lot from being able to switch to whichever newer model works best, even if it comes from a different vendor. I try to keep my whole workflow agent-agnostic, so I have no switching cost. It’s far from clear which model will win in the end, and as a user, you’re in a much better position if you can work with any model available rather than being locked into one.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Neovim</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Neovim has been my primary editor for a long time, and it’s a critical part of staying fully keyboard-driven inside the terminal. You might ask, “But I use agents now. Why do I need an IDE?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I use it to quickly examine the file system, review diffs, and make small edits when needed. A few plugins do most of the heavy lifting:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I don’t let my terminal emulator manage tabs, because I manage all my sessions, windows, tabs, and panes in tmux instead. It’s one of the most powerful primitives in my whole setup, and it unlocks a few things at once:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Splitting my terminal window into panes the way I like</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Driving the entire terminal experience from the keyboard</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Persisting the working sessions and layout</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Accessing the same session from my other devices (more on that later)</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A popular alternative is Zellij, but tmux has worked well enough that I haven’t switched. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Basic Prompting</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We’re now in the terminal, and the agent is waiting for instructions. All I have to do is write a prompt. Sounds easy, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Actually, how you write your prompts is one of the biggest levers on both the velocity of your work and the quality of the outcome. So let me share a few things that made a big difference for me.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Using Voice Input</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Typing was my primary input method for decades. But over the last couple of years, speech recognition models have really changed the game. You can now run high-quality models locally on your Mac, for free, that generate output extremely fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>You talk a lot faster than you type, so moving to voice as your primary input is one of the easiest ways to greatly improve your productivity. It applies to prompting your agents, but also to anything else that used to require typing. This post, for example, is mostly written by voice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The solution I use is</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88a3c673-77da-4586-ac31-721ca69d0953?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> OpenSuperWhisper</span></a><span>, which is completely free and runs the Whisper model (turbo v3 large) locally. I set a hotkey to trigger it, and now I can just talk wherever I could type. There are plenty of other free and paid options that give a great experience as well.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Delegating like a Manager</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For many new tech leads and people managers, the first struggle is delegation. The same thing happens with how you interact with agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most common mistakes I see people make about delegation to both humans and agents are:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>asking for an action, not an outcome;</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>not explaining the “why.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>taking back control.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Take “rename this variable.” It’s a valid prompt, but it has a couple of problems:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The agent finishes in a few seconds and waits for you again. It barely saves more time than doing it yourself, and you’re still the bottleneck.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>There’s no “why.” Do you want it renamed for readability? To follow a team convention? Because of a future plan you haven’t mentioned? Without the why, there’s no room for the agent to suggest something better, and it won’t know how to do it right next time.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If you were following a convention, a better prompt would be: “Let’s audit this part of our codebase and make sure our variable naming follows this convention <link_to_document>.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That explains the rationale, gives the necessary context, and asks for an outcome instead of an action. The agent can run longer, get more done in a way that’s aligned with your goal, and respect that convention for the rest of the session instead of creating more problems for you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The other failure mode is taking back control. When a mistake happens, people immediately think of doing it themselves. This happens to new tech leads working with a junior engineer. They could do the job faster by taking over, but in doing so, they make themselves the bottleneck and fail to scale. People hit the exact same wall with AI: they see an agent do something wrong and revert to doing it manually, and they never truly unlock the leverage agents offer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The right approach is to give feedback and help the other party improve. With agents, this is actually easier. You can write directly into the agent’s memory file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), or ask the agent to reflect on its mistake and update that file so the same thing doesn’t happen again.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Planning Complex Work</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The feature I’m building right now is image input. I want the chat box in Hi Bit to accept a pasted image from the clipboard, or open a file picker or camera. This is a bit more than I think the agent can one-shot the way I want. In the beginning, I also didn’t know exactly where the button should go or what the attached images should look like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This happens a lot: problems where I genuinely can’t describe the full solution up front. It could be a new project from scratch, a major refactor, or a big feature on an existing system. In those cases, I work with the agent to write a plan first.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There’s a school of thought in the agentic community that’s against technical planning. They prefer to “just talk to your agent” instead.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I went the other way, and here’s why. When you just talk to your agent, you have to stay in an interactive session. You get constantly pulled back into the conversation, and after a few rounds, it’s hard to keep track of what the actual plan is. A long wall of text in the terminal is also painful to parse and hard to give targeted feedback on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Instead, I spend a concentrated chunk of time up front getting the plan into a confident state, so I can hand it off for a fully autonomous implementation without jumping back in until it’s done. That’s also what frees me up to run other tasks in parallel without constant context switching.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For a long time, I did this by asking the agent to write a proposal in a markdown file, then questioning it and iterating. That worked, but I have something better now. Inspired by an article on using HTML as interactive artifacts, I built a tool called</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93ebbef0-158e-4d01-adb9-5bbe283effa3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> Lavish Editor</span></a><span> to collaborate with the agent on anything complex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So instead of “draft a technical plan in a markdown file,” I say “draft a technical plan using npx lavish-axi.” Lavish guides the agent to render the plan as an interactive HTML page and opens it in my browser. It even encourages the agent to match the look and feel of the current project, so the plan for a UI feature looks visually consistent with the real app, which makes options far easier to judge.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" Being able to interact with a plan this richly, instead of editing a markdown file, turned out to be a big productivity boost, and it’s not limited to planning. I now use Lavish for brainstorming, reviewing changes, data reports, and anything else that benefits from a visual artifact and tight back-and-forth. It’s been a game-changer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Implementation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once the plan is clear, the implementation is fully autonomous, and there’s honestly not much for me to do except wait for the agent to ping when it’s done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The one thing worth mentioning over here is that for every project, I spend a lot of effort making sure the agent can validate its own change end-to-end. As an example, for Hi Bit, I keep explicit instructions in the repo’s AGENTS.md for how to exercise the app, so changes like this get validated by the agent before they come back to me. I can often watch it test its own work in real time by driving the real app, attaching an image, and checking how the new button actually behaves.</span></p><div justify"><span>Occasionally, a task is so complex that it doesn’t fit well in a single context window. If I just let the agent grind on it, it fills its context, fires off very large requests, and eventually compacts to free space, sometimes losing important context in the process. The newer /goal command in Codex and Claude Code helps a bit, but I’ve been using something better since well before it existed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I call it </span><strong><span>good night, have fun</span></strong><span>: gnhf for short. It’s a dead-simple, long-running orchestrator I built for running big tasks overnight; you invoke it with gnhf <your objective>.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>Under the hood, it works similarly to the Ralph Loop and Autoresearch patterns. It breaks the task into small steps, and each step runs in a fresh context window seeded with a common base context plus the learnings from previous steps. Failed attempts roll back automatically, and the next attempt takes the failure into account. I can also set a token budget so I don’t wake up bankrupt. When I come back, there’s a branch with well-organized commits and a notes.md file summarizing what was done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I reach for gnhf in three kinds of situations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Implement a massive plan: gnhf “fully implement this plan…”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Improve a measurable metric such as reducing lines of code, increasing test coverage, cutting startup latency, or page load time: gnhf “improve <this metric> while keeping product functionality unchanged.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Run lots of offline experiments when you have an evaluator capable of scoring each attempt. For one project, I generated a game map by running 50+ layout experiments and scoring each through a gameplay simulation. Babysitting those by hand would have taken weeks.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Validation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Back to the image task: the agent has done the work, and it has produced a big change. Now what? This is where many people hit the real bottleneck: code review. There’s simply too much code to read, and reviewing it isn’t the fun part of the job.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’m increasingly convinced that working with agents means acting like an engineering manager. Most managers rarely review code directly. They have the team review each other’s work, and before anything ships, they ask for evidence that it actually works. It’s the same with AI, except the developer is the manager and the agents are the team. You have to get good at using agents to scrutinize agents’ code, get them to self-correct, and get them to produce artifacts that demonstrate the feature really works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’ve experimented a lot here, and a few things turned out to matter most:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Run the reviewer agent in a fresh context window. If you review in the same session that wrote the code, the agent is biased by what it just did and assumes it was intended. It’s like asking someone to check their own work. They’ll catch some things, but it’s far weaker than a real peer review.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Escalate ambiguous, product-changing decisions to the human. Reviewers make mistakes, too. If you let the agent auto-fix every finding as if it’s all valid, it can drift into rabbit holes away from what you actually want. Keeping those decisions with the human keeps you in control of the ambiguity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Force end-to-end evidence. Today’s frontier models lean heavily on unit tests to validate changes, probably because of how they’re trained. But I’ve seen countless cases where every unit test passes, and the product is still buggy. You have to make the agent prove the change works E2E.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I packaged all of this into an open-source tool I built called no-mistakes, which I now run on the image change. First, I use the neogit plugin to quickly scan the diff and make sure it’s roughly aligned with what I asked. Sometimes an agent goes in a completely wrong direction, and that’s obvious at a glance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If it looks reasonable, I run </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">no-mistakes -y</span><span> and it handles the rest: commit with a conventional message into a descriptively named branch, rebase onto the latest main and resolve conflicts, spin up agents to peer-review and self-correct obvious bugs, test the change E2E and produce evidence, close documentation gaps, fix linting, push, open a well-structured PR, and babysit CI until it’s green.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of it runs autonomously except for the decisions it deliberately escalates to me.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>This validation pipeline has become one of the most critical pieces of my whole workflow. My own stats show that 68% of the changes I pushed through the no-mistakes tool had bugs in them. I genuinely can’t imagine what my codebase would look like without it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Parallelization</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>With a fully autonomous implement-and-validate pipeline, a single task can take a while, and that’s a good thing, because it frees me up to run more things at once.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Handling Agent Status</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In tmux, this means opening a new window. Terminal tabs achieve the same parallelism. The important part is keeping those tabs visible and showing each agent’s status in the tab title. Claude Code and Codex do this out of the box; for harnesses that don’t, I wrote small plugins to do the same, and I made the </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">no-mistakes</span><span> tool report its status as a custom title too.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That one detail is what lets me run many sessions without going insane. At any moment, I can see which agents are running, which are done, and which need my input. A couple of tmux keystrokes jump me to any tab.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Managing Worktrees</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The other problem with running agents in parallel is that they step on each other’s toes when they share a directory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Git worktrees exist to solve this. A worktree is an efficient clone of the same repo in another directory where you can work in parallel. But worktrees carry a lot of cognitive load: where to put them, how to name them, create a new one or reuse an old one, which are in use, which have dependencies installed, and whether env files are ready. What I actually want to think about is the work, not where to do it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So I built another open-source tool named treehouse. You’re in a repo, you want to start a parallel task, you run treehouse, and it drops you into a ready worktree. Behind the scenes, it manages a pool of worktrees, tracks which are free, reuses an idle one when possible (so dependencies, build artifacts, and env files are already there), and makes sure it’s synced with the latest main before dropping you in. I don’t think about any of that. I simply run the treehouse tool and start working.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
