item.description: Stop using JWTs

item.title: publishing
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
publishing

Hamed Salameh

Saving data and publishing a message are two separate operations, so a crash between them can silently lose events. The Outbox Pattern fixes this by writing messages to a database table in the same transaction as your business data, then using a background dispatcher to publish them to the broker. This gives you at-least-once delivery without any distributed coordination. Hamed walks through a full .NET 10 implementation using EF Core, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, and MassTransit. See one of the few solutions purpose-built for generating real
item.description: publishing

item.title: vulnerability reports
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
vulnerability reports

Nikolche Kolev

.NET 10 now removes platform-provided packages from dependency graphs by default. Many libraries pull in packages like System.Text.Json as dependencies even when the .NET runtime already includes a newer version, causing false vulnerability warnings. Package pruning strips these redundant entries at restore time, cutting false-positive vulnerability reports by 70% and reducing restore times by up to 50%.
item.description: vulnerability reports

item.title: EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way

Anton Martyniuk

Wrapping EF Core in a repository layer adds unnecessary complexity since DbContext already implements those patterns. Using DbContext directly in application use cases keeps code simpler, easier to read, and faster to change. Tests improve too, as running against a real database with tools like Testcontainers catches bugs that mocked repositories miss. Custom repositories still make sense for complex shared queries, multiple data sources, or strict team conventions.
item.description: EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way

item.title: New lines are more than \r and \n
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
New lines are more than \r and \n

Gérald Barré

Most developers only think of \r\n and \n as line breaks, but Unicode defines several more, including \u0085, \u2028, and \u2029. Ignoring these can cause parsing bugs when handling text from office tools, legacy systems, or cross-platform sources. In .NET, you can handle all cases using a regex pattern, string.ReplaceLineEndings, or the SplitLines helper from Meziantou.Framework. item.description: New lines are more than \r and \n

item.title: rows without the wait
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
rows without the wait

Chris Woodruff

Inserting large volumes of data with a simple foreach loop works fine locally but falls apart in production due to slow change tracking, too many database round trips, and high memory use. EF Core 10's native AddRange with a single SaveChangesAsync call solves most of this through batching and fixes the change tracker overhead. For higher volumes or complex parent-child data, Entity Framework Extensions adds bulk insert methods that match raw SQL speed while keeping EF Core model integration. 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Big models cost more. Small models do less. Here's how SLMs and LLMs differ across the dimensions that matter in production: </span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Architecture: SLMs are usually under 10B parameters and run on a laptop or phone. LLMs sit at 10B+ with deeper layers and more attention heads, built for broad reasoning across tasks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Task Complexity: SLMs work well on simple tasks but fail on complex multiple reasoning steps. LLMs handle difficult math, multi-step code, and long-horizon planning. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Long Context Recall: SLMs lose the thread across long documents or extended conversations. LLMs reliably track and connect information across large inputs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Latency and Cost: SLMs run on consumer hardware with low response times and significantly lower inference costs. LLMs require GPU and carry higher costs per request.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Deployment and Privacy: SLMs run on-device or on-premise. LLMs are typically cloud-hosted, which adds data governance complexity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);"><span>Where each fits:</span><br><span>SLMs: on-device assistants, real-time classification, or privacy-sensitive applications</span><br><span>LLMs: complex reasoning, agent workflows, or broad knowledge tasks.</span></span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);"><span>Are you using SLMs, LLMs, or a hybrid setup in production?</span><br></span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Single Agent vs. Multi-Agent Architecture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Some tasks need a single agent. item.title: Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership

Will Larson

“This post documents the new rules I’ve revised my approach to engineering leadership around, and then talks through the specific projects I’ve worked on over the past year that caused me to believe in these rules.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership

item.title: Don't Stack Weaknesses
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Don't Stack Weaknesses

Yue Zhao

“The real damage happens when you stack weaknesses - when a leader is weak at something and their direct reports are weak at the same thing. This is a disaster, and it happens far more often than you’d think. Part of the reason for this is that leaders tend to hire people with the same skills they have. They’ll dress it up as hiring for “values” instead of “skills” so it doesn’t look like they’re cloning themselves - but people ultimately search for and evaluate the things they’re good at.”

#Management Hiring
item.description: Don't Stack Weaknesses

item.title: Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning

Steve Huynh

“Every “yes” is a check written against the future that has to be cleared. And clearing checks written by “powerful Us” is especially tough. Why? Because, by definition, we are only average most of the time. This article provides a guide to recognizing overextension in ourselves, so that, before we commit to things, we can be sure that we are only taking on what we can hold.”

#CareerGrowth DecisionMaking Wellbeing
item.description: Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning

item.title: The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring

Scott Kennedy

“In this generation we call them “AI Natives”. The advantage is that there are no old habits to break or reframe. Many experienced folks are open minded and can do it, but many resist. New grads don’t know the difference, their learning came in parallel to having these tools. We see it in interviews regularly, new grads can use AI coding tools incredibly well.”

#IndustryTrends AI Hiring
item.description: The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring

item.title: Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?

Gergely Orosz

“In this article, we walk through what’s happened, and ask what’s going through the minds of leadership who are reducing software engineering there from the profit center that it was between 2004 until very recently, to the disdained cost center that it has become in just a few weeks.”

#IndustryTrends Leadership
item.description: Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?

item.title: SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort

Anders Murphy

“The defining characteristic of a B+ Tree is that it is ordered. Sequential writes are fast. Random data works against this thrashing pages, causing page splits and tree re-balancing. It's not a good time. But, we are batching the data already. So what if we sort it before we insert?”

#Database DeepDive Performance
item.description: SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort

item.title: Agentic Code Review
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Agentic Code Review

Addy Osmani

“Stop reviewing everything to the same depth. Spend scarce human attention only where being wrong is costly, and let cheap deterministic gates and AI reviewers handle the rest. The organizing idea is to match review effort to the cost of being wrong, push the cheap deterministic work as early as possible, and reserve human attention for what only humans can do.”

#CodeReview AI Agents
item.description: Agentic Code Review

20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Observability for Beginners: Logs, Metrics, Traces, and Everything Around Them</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">A running service generates events constantly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Requests arrive, functions run, errors appear, and each one is a thing that happened at a specific time with a specific context and a specific outcome.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Logs, metrics, and traces are three ways of looking at this same stream. A log captures one event as a line of text, a metric counts or aggregates many events, and a trace links related events as they move across services. Most of the concepts in observability, including cardinality, sampling, and correlation, are consequences of this structure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">In this article, we will look at the basics of observability in detail with concepts like logs, Antithesis enables teams like Jane Street, Fly.io,  and the etcd community to use agents safely and ship better code, faster. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e3f52f76-c491-4ab3-a2df-1378b210b367?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Learn more</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ce6678b-81cf-4dda-af12-01e664558b1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">WorkOS</a></strong><span> – make your app and agents Enterprise Ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ce6678b-81cf-4dda-af12-01e664558b1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Get started.</a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b14ef9-0cbb-42be-95c7-4293f9b6897e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">turbopuffer</a></strong><span> – a vector and full-text search engine built on object storage. It’s fast, cheap, and extremely scalable. The teams building the smartest AI products out there — Cursor, Notion, Cognition, Anthropic — they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b14ef9-0cbb-42be-95c7-4293f9b6897e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">all run on turbopuffer</a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Robert Erez is a principal engineer at Octopus Deploy, and a longtime expert in CI/CD, deployment systems, and software delivery. Rob and I were also once colleagues on the Skype web team, working on large-scale deployments and release processes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of</span><em> The</em><span> </span><em>Pragmatic Engineer</em><span>, I sit down with Rob to discuss how teams deploy software safely and efficiently at scale. We cover Kubernetes, GitOps, platform engineering, progressive delivery, feature flags, cloud development environments, and the growing role of AI in CI/CD workflows. We also get into the tradeoffs in different deployment approaches, why self-hosted software still matters for some organizations, and the recent evolution of software delivery practices.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Key observations on deployments and CI/CD from the conversation with Rob</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here are 10 interesting takeaways from our chat:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9ba451e-654c-49a4-95ed-97b607ff898d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2x0eq5oDOJY" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. Roll forward, never backwards. </strong><span>When a system has state – which typically means it uses databases – then doing a rollback can leave the code talking to a schema that’s no longer in sync. Rob’s advice is to not treat a failure in v2 as a trip back to v1, but rather as a push to v3 with the fix in it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. GitOps isn’t actually about Git.</strong><span> None of the four pillars of GitOps – 1) declarative, 2) versioned and immutable, 3) pulled, not pushed, 4) continuously reconciled  – require Git, although Git can work under these constraints. Yet, the term  ‘GitOps’ has made the industry dogmatic about cramming </span><em>everything</em><span> into a repo – even things like secrets that absolutely shouldn’t be there!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. Continuous deployment can be overkill; continuous delivery is more practical. </strong><span>Shipping every single change to prod (continuous deployment) is not as necessary as many people think, Rob says, and there’s often more value in continuous delivery, where changes flow through testing and the deployment process itself is validated. With continuous delivery, you can decide whether to push to production automatically, or click a button once a week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. Feature toggles are a better safety net than rollbacks.</strong><span> When something breaks in production, reaching for a toggle to switch a feature off enables you to “stop the bleeding” and then calmly diagnose an issue. Rolling back a feature flag is less nerve-jangling than scrambling to force a redeployment in the middle of the night!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>5. One problem with feature flags is that they’re addictive.</strong><span> On the other hand, the ease with which feature flags are added can create a hygiene crisis if they’re continuously added, but not removed. Treat feature-toggle cleanups like a form of gardening and “weed” rolled-out toggles from the codebase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>6. A Git repo can be a bottleneck at scale.</strong><span> Rob mentions that some companies run thousands of independent Kubernetes clusters that pull state from a Git repository. But such clusters can get throttled by the repo, forcing them into workarounds. Pull-based GitOps doesn’t scale infinitely for free.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>7. A sizable number of major institutions remain on-prem – and this won’t change. </strong><span>Banks, other financial bodies, and governments, demand full control over their hardware, upgrades, and downtime. That’s why Rob expects this segment won’t move to cloud-based SaaS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>8. Platform teams work at larger companies. </strong><span>These teams earn their keep in big organizations with multiple teams and projects because they offer ways of bringing sanity and focus.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>9. There’s a trend of ephemeral environments replacing test/staging environments. </strong><span>Companies used to have a few testers fighting over a handful of static test environments, but today, it’s trivial to spin up a full environment, per-feature branch, pre-merge. This is an “ephemeral” environment for evaluating that things work, which is then torn down once something is merged. It helps speed up the feedback process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>10. AI shifts the CI/CD calculus from speed to risk.</strong><span> Today, shaving ten minutes off the CI build-time matters because a long-running build blocks human devs. But this time saving will be insignificant when an AI agent writes most of the code and “babysits” a slow pipeline without context switching. Then, the new priority will be to reduce the risk of an AI agent shipping a bug to production, so it will make much more sense to run extra, more thorough, tests – and also even slower ones.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe
